title: Which pair of tests really checks for twenty four?
description: Prime factorisation shows why twelve passes the tests for four and six but is not divisible by twenty four, and why the tests for three and eight never let such a number through. Keeko's doubt is that passing the tests for four and six always works for twenty four.
teaching_notes: One idea: two tests together check for the least common multiple of the two numbers, and four and six share a two, so they only check for twelve. Watch for students who multiply the two test numbers and expect the product to be checked.

source: Use prime factorisation to explain why 12 passes the tests for 4 and 6 but is not divisible by 24
video_script.why: A learner sees with prime factors why the tests for four and six check only for twelve, while the tests for three and eight check for twenty four.
video_script.substitution: the book's own numbers: twelve, twenty four, and the pairs four and six, three and eight
video_script.anchor: the prime factors of 12, 4, 6, 3, 8 and 24 written as products of primes
video_script.wrong_answer: a number that passes the tests for four and six is always divisible by twenty four
video_script.wrong_move: multiplies four and six to get twenty four and trusts the two tests to check for the product
video_script.payoff_line: Four and six only check for twelve, and three and eight check for twenty four.

final_answer.value: 4 and 6 only test for 12, their LCM; 3 and 8 test for 24
final_answer.spoken: the tests for four and six only check for twelve, and the tests for three and eight check for twenty four

hold_back: 4 and 6 only test for 12, their LCM; 3 and 8 test for 24
maths_rules: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3; 4 = 2 × 2 and 6 = 2 × 3 both divide it, so 12 passes the tests for 4 and 6
24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 needs three 2s and one 3; 12 has only two 2s
4 and 6 share a 2, so a number passing both holds 2 × 2 × 3 only, which is 12
8 = 2 × 2 × 2 and 3 share no factor, so a number passing both holds 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 24
the least common multiple of 4 and 6 is 12; of 3 and 8 is 24
video_script.design: One idea: two tests check for their least common multiple, and prime factors show why. Assumes prime factorisation. The prime factor lines stay on the board all video.

<bookmark mark='ask'/>One pair of tests is four and six. The other pair is three and eight.
Which pair really checks for twenty four?

narration: <bookmark mark='prime'/>Prime factorisation writes a number as primes multiplied together. Twenty four is two times two times two times three.
<bookmark mark='need'/>A number is divisible by twenty four only when it holds three twos and a three.

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find why twelve passes the tests for four and six. We also find why the tests for three and eight work.

marks.six: 6 = 2 × 3 is matched with a 2 and the 3 of 12

narration: <bookmark mark='twelve'/>Step one, twelve is two times two times three.
<bookmark mark='four'/>Four is two times two, and it divides twelve.
<bookmark mark='six'/>Six is two times three, and it divides twelve too. Twelve passes both tests.

beats.on_screen: 24 needs three 2s and a 3; 12 has two 2s. 4 and 6 share a 2, so they ask only for 2 × 2 × 3

narration: <bookmark mark='need'/>Step two, twenty four needs three twos, but twelve has only two.
<bookmark mark='share'/>Four and six share a two. A number counts that two only once.
<bookmark mark='only'/>The two tests ask only for two times two times three, so they let twelve through.

beats.on_screen: 8 = 2 × 2 × 2 and 3 share no factor, so passing both gives 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 24. LCM of 4 and 6 is 12; LCM of 3 and 8 is 24

marks.eight: 8 = 2 × 2 × 2 and 3 are written with nothing shared
marks.lcm: the words least common multiple (LCM) appear
marks.vals: LCM of 4 and 6 is 12, and LCM of 3 and 8 is 24, are written

narration: <bookmark mark='eight'/>Step three, eight is two times two times two, and three shares no factor with it.
<bookmark mark='hold'/>A number that passes both tests holds three twos and a three. That makes twenty four.
<bookmark mark='lcm'/>The smallest number that two numbers both divide into is called their least common multiple.
<bookmark mark='vals'/>It is twelve for four and six, and twenty four for three and eight.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 4 and 6 only test for 12, their LCM; 3 and 8 test for 24
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Four and six only check for twelve, and three and eight check for twenty four.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks a number that passes the tests for four and six is always divisible by twenty four.
Four times six is twenty four, says Keeko.
<bookmark mark='twelve'/>But twelve passes both tests, and twenty four does not go into twelve.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Four and six share a two, but multiplying four by six counts that two twice. Three and eight share nothing, so they work.
